But honest serious question I have at least two devices that were water damaged beyond repair am I okay to throw those away without worrying about data being recovered?

Ahh, it kind of depends how paranoid you need to be, but the real answer would be "no, you would not be ok just throwing it away". Unless the storage media were sufficiently destroyed by water damage -- which there's really no way for you to tell -- data could still be extracted by relatively simple means.

If you have/had sensitive data stored on the device, you'd probably want to open the device and remove the memory modules (de-solder them from the board), and physically destroy the media via Disintegrate, Pulverize, Melt, and Incinerate (for example, burn it in a fire or smash it with a hammer.) You can then safely recycle the remaining components. In the future it would be advisable to use full-disk encryption so that any remaining data located within the flash memory is unusable without a sufficiently complex password or private key.

Check out: http://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-88r1.pdf

The typical Hard Disk Drive is considered 'clean' or 'sanitized' by Department of Defense standards after several randomized complete write-throughs. Some institutions actually put each hard drive through a drill press or smash the platters, or degauss them to make them physically unreadable or unusable. Flash memory is a little bit different in how it operates, but it is considered safest to physically destroy the media.

Edit: If you're interested, here's a good write-up of the difference between HDD and SSD sanitization: https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/fast11/tech/full_papers/Wei.pdf

Edit 2: Don't just burn your entire device, especially without removing the battery first. It can release very harmful fumes. It is far better to only destroy the memory modules, as that is the only component capable of long-term storage. Then it is safe to recycle the remaining components.
